Q: How StateFlow.collectAsState() works A:

A Flow in general is an observable stream of values. That is compatible to the concept of Compose State, which represents a value that can be observed for changes. collectAsState1 simply converts a Flow into a Compose State.

That means that whenever the Flow emits2 a new value, the corresponding State object changes its value and triggers a recomposition. That works because internally, collectAsState launches a coroutine to wait for new values. That coroutine is usually suspended most of the time and only wakes up when a new value was emitted into the Flow. It receives the new value in a callback and updates the Compose State object, which in turn triggers a recomposition, keeping the UI up-to-date.

Your assumption is basically correct, except that collectAsState doesn't actively access the value property, it receives the new value in a callback. But that's just an implementation detail that doesn't matter when you just use the function.

1 As a reminder, when you use any other Flow implementation than a MutableStateFlow you should use collectAsStateWithLifecycle instead of collectAsState, that saves resources by stopping the Flow when it isn't needed. You don't need that for a MutableStateFlow because that is special in that it isn't running its own coroutine to produce values, so there is nothing that needs be stopped. Its probably easier to always use collectAsStateWithLifecycle though, the overhead is minimal and you decouple your Compose code from the view model implementation.

2 The MutableStateFlow you use emits a new value whenever you write to the value property or use the update method. StateFlows have the additional semantic that they drop redundant values. So if you write the same value again, nothing happens.

Q: How to implement Hilt correctly? A:

The Hilt version you use is simply too old.

With AGP 9, some things need to be done differently now. Specifically the way the Hilt plugin hooks into the compilation process has changed, and the first version working with AGP 9 is 2.59.

Just update to the newest version (at the time of writing) by changing this in your version catalog:

hilt = "2.59.2"

You can now use alias(libs.plugins.hilt) again in your gradle file. After a Gradle sync your app should be able to be built again.

Looking at your build files, I want to highlight another change with AGP 9: Kotlin comes now built-in. You do not need to specify the Kotlin plugin org.jetbrains.kotlin.android anymore. To be more precise, it is incompatible now and cannot be used anymore. You already commented it out in your app level gradle file, but you should also remove alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.android) apply false from your project level gradle file and also remove the entry in the version catalog. Delete this line:

kotlin-android = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.android", version.ref = "kotlin" }

The Kotlin version itself (kotlin = "2.2.10") is still needed for the Compose plugin. This superseeds what AGP 9 would otherwise fall back to. By default that is (also) 2.2.10. But you can always use a newer version. The newest one at the time of writing is this:

kotlin = "2.3.21"

Q: Dataframe sorting and column count A:

The easiest way is to make DayOfWeek an ordered categorical column, then use groupby().size() to count each combination.

days = [
    'Monday', 'Tuesday', 'Wednesday', 'Thursday',
    'Friday', 'Saturday', 'Sunday'
]

coffee_dataset['DayOfWeek'] = pd.Categorical(
    coffee_dataset['DayOfWeek'],
    categories=days,
    ordered=True
)

result = (
    coffee_dataset
    .groupby(['DayOfWeek', 'CoffeeType'], observed=False)
    .size()
    .reset_index(name='Count')
    .sort_values(['DayOfWeek', 'CoffeeType'])
)

print(result)

Using .agg({'CoffeeType': 'count'}) isn't ideal here because you're aggregating the CoffeeType column itself. .size() gives you a separate count column instead. The categorical column also prevents the days from being sorted alphabetically.

Q: Ideal Android Studio Kotlin gitignore A:

The .gitignore file for a Java project and a Kotlin project can have some differences but they are likely to be minor. It could be depending on the frameworks used, the IDE, the build tools (Maven or Gradle) or the dependencies.

If you use Android Studio, it will automatically generate a rather complete gitignore.

But I can tell you the most important elements you need to exclude :

  • /.idea : This directory contains project-specific settings and configuration files for Android Studio. You can exclude this directory as it is not required for building the project.

  • /build : This directory contains the compiled code and build artifacts. You can exclude this directory as it can be rebuilt from the source code.

  • *.iml : This file is generated by Android Studio and contains information about the development module. You can exclude this file as it can be regenerated.

  • local.properties : This file contains the path to the Android SDK. You can exclude this file as it is specific to your local environment.

For example for a new empty project Android Studio generated me this gitignore:

*.iml
.gradle
/local.properties
/.idea/caches
/.idea/libraries
/.idea/modules.xml
/.idea/workspace.xml
/.idea/navEditor.xml
/.idea/assetWizardSettings.xml
.DS_Store
/build
/captures
.externalNativeBuild
.cxx
local.properties

Hope that will be useful!
